subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Electricity and Magnetism Reading
subtitle: Electric charge, circuits, magnetism, electromagnets, motors, generators, and evidence-based explanations.
description: Reading passages and comprehension questions grounded in the source study pack. Students retrieve facts, interpret data, explain circuit and magnetism patterns, and connect electromagnetism to real devices.

data.sourcePassage: Matter is made of atoms. Atoms contain protons with positive charge, electrons with negative charge, and neutrons with no charge. Most objects are neutral because they have balanced positive and negative charges. An object becomes charged when electrons move from one object to another. When a balloon is rubbed on hair, electrons may transfer, leaving the balloon and hair oppositely charged. Like charges repel, while opposite charges attract. Static electricity is a buildup of charge that is not flowing continuously through a circuit. Hair standing up, clothes sticking together, small shocks from carpet, and lightning all involve charge buildup and electric forces.

questions.question: Which particle usually moves when objects become charged by rubbing?
questions.modelAnswer: Electrons usually move from one object to another.

questions.question: What happens to two objects with opposite electric charges?
questions.modelAnswer: They attract each other.

questions.question: Why is a rubbed balloon able to stick to hair or a wall?
questions.modelAnswer: Rubbing can transfer electrons, leaving charge imbalances. Electric forces can then attract the balloon to nearby objects.

questions.question: Which example from the passage is static electricity?
questions.modelAnswer: Clothes sticking together after drying is static electricity.

questions.question: How does lightning connect to the idea of electric fields?
questions.modelAnswer: Charge buildup can make an electric field strong enough for charge to move suddenly through air as a spark.

data.sourcePassage: Electric current is the flow of electric charge. For a steady current to flow, a circuit needs a complete closed path and an energy source. A simple circuit may include a battery, wires, a switch, and a load such as a bulb or motor. If the path is broken, the circuit is open and current stops. Charges do not get used up by the bulb. Instead, electrical energy is transferred from the battery to the load. In a flashlight, chemical energy in the battery helps provide voltage. Current flows through the bulb or LED, and electrical energy changes into light energy and thermal energy.

questions.question: What two things are needed for steady current to flow in a simple circuit?
questions.modelAnswer: A complete closed path and an energy source are needed.

questions.question: What is the load in a simple bulb circuit?
questions.modelAnswer: The bulb is the load because it uses electrical energy.

questions.question: Why does a bulb not light in an open circuit?
questions.modelAnswer: An open circuit has a gap, so current cannot complete the path through the bulb.

questions.question: Correct this statement: The bulb uses up the current.
questions.modelAnswer: The bulb does not use up current. Current flows around the circuit, while energy is transferred to the bulb and changed into light and thermal energy.

questions.question: Which energy change best describes a flashlight?
options: Light energy to chemical energy only
Chemical energy to electrical energy to light and thermal energy
questions.modelAnswer: Chemical energy changes to electrical energy, then light and thermal energy.

data.sourceTitle: Current, Voltage, Resistance, Series, and Parallel Circuits
data.targetTitle: Current, Voltage, Resistance, Series, and Parallel Circuits
data.sourcePassage: Circuit behavior can be described using current, voltage, and resistance. Current is the flow of charge, voltage is the push that moves charge, and resistance is opposition to current. In one investigation, voltage stayed at 6 volts while resistance changed. At 2 ohms the current was 3.0 amps, at 3 ohms it was 2.0 amps, at 6 ohms it was 1.0 amp, and at 12 ohms it was 0.5 amps. The pattern was clear: as resistance increased, current decreased. Circuit arrangement also matters. A series circuit has one path for current, so one break stops the circuit. A parallel circuit has multiple branches, so other branches can often keep working if one branch breaks.

questions.question: In the resistance investigation, what value stayed the same in every trial?
questions.modelAnswer: The voltage stayed the same at 6 volts.

questions.question: What happened to current as resistance increased?
questions.modelAnswer: Current decreased as resistance increased.

questions.question: Which resistance had a current of 1.0 amp?
questions.modelAnswer: A resistance of 6 ohms had a current of 1.0 amp.

questions.question: Why can one broken bulb stop all bulbs in a simple series circuit?
questions.modelAnswer: A series circuit has only one path. Removing or breaking one bulb opens that path, so current cannot flow through the whole loop.

questions.question: Why are parallel circuits useful in homes?
questions.modelAnswer: Parallel circuits give devices separate branches, so devices can operate independently and one broken branch does not necessarily stop the others.

data.sourcePassage: A magnet produces a magnetic field. Magnetic forces can push or pull on other magnets and on some materials. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Like magnetic poles repel, while opposite poles attract. Magnetic field lines are closest together near the poles, where the field is usually strongest. Not all metals are strongly attracted to magnets. Iron, nickel, cobalt, and many steels are ferromagnetic, but copper and aluminum usually are not strongly attracted to ordinary magnets. Earth also has a magnetic field. A compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with Earth’s magnetic field and helps people navigate.

questions.question: Which pair of magnetic poles repels?
questions.modelAnswer: North and north repel because like poles repel.

questions.question: Name one ferromagnetic material from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Iron, nickel, cobalt, or many steels are ferromagnetic materials.

questions.question: What evidence could show that a magnetic field is present around a magnet?
questions.modelAnswer: Iron filings forming a pattern around the magnet or a compass needle turning near it would show that a magnetic field is present.

questions.question: Why is the statement all metals are magnetic inaccurate?
questions.modelAnswer: Only some metals are strongly attracted to ordinary magnets. Iron, nickel, cobalt, and many steels are attracted, but copper and aluminum usually are not.

questions.question: How does a compass connect everyday navigation to Earth's magnetic field?
questions.modelAnswer: A compass needle is magnetized, so it lines up with Earth's magnetic field. This alignment helps people find direction.

data.sourcePassage: Electricity and magnetism are connected. Electric current creates a magnetic field. If wire is wrapped into a coil, the magnetic field becomes stronger and more like the field of a bar magnet. A simple electromagnet can be made with a battery, insulated wire, and an iron nail. In one investigation, 5 coils lifted 2 paper clips, 10 coils lifted 5, 15 coils lifted 8, and 20 coils lifted 11. The data support the claim that more coils can make the electromagnet stronger. Magnetism can also help make electricity. A generator uses motion and a changing magnetic field to produce current. A motor does the reverse energy change by using electrical energy and magnetic forces to create motion.

questions.question: What three basic materials can make a simple electromagnet?
questions.modelAnswer: A battery, insulated wire, and an iron nail can make a simple electromagnet.

questions.question: What claim is supported by the paper clip data?
options: More coils can increase electromagnet strength
Fewer coils always make stronger magnets
questions.modelAnswer: Increasing the number of coils can increase electromagnet strength.

questions.question: How many paper clips were lifted with 15 coils?
questions.modelAnswer: The electromagnet with 15 coils lifted 8 paper clips.

questions.question: Why can an electromagnet often be turned on and off?
questions.modelAnswer: It depends on electric current. Closing the circuit lets current create magnetism, and opening the circuit stops the current so the magnetism becomes much weaker.

questions.question: Compare the main energy changes in a motor and a generator.
questions.modelAnswer: A motor changes electrical energy into motion, while a generator changes motion into electrical energy using a changing magnetic field.
